title: Money, Enterprise and Being a Customer
overview: Level 1 Unit 18 taught you to report a fault and ask for it to be fixed. This unit is the level above: the expressions English uses to measure uncountable things, the vocabulary of price and contract, and the structure of a complaint that gets a remedy rather than an apology. It ends with two complaints about the same problem, one of which was paid and one of which was not.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 3 is the one that decides whether you get anything.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is two complaints and their outcomes.
Do the Practice. Practice 3 is the diagnostic — does this ask for a remedy?
Record yourself making a complaint that asks for something specific.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
Three patterns, and the third one is worth more money than the other two put together.
First pattern: partitive expressions. These are the words English uses to measure things you cannot count.
In Level 1 Unit 6 you had a few of these — a packet of, a bottle of, a slice of. This is the wider system, and it splits into two kinds.
The first kind measures physical things. A portion of, a batch of, a bundle of, a sheet of, a strip of, a length of, a drop of, a grain of.
These are learned with the substance and there is no rule. A grain of rice, a slice of bread, a bar of soap, a sheet of paper. You cannot deduce them, and when you do not know one, the general-purpose word is piece — a piece of paper, a piece of equipment, a piece of advice. Piece works for almost anything and it always sounds acceptable, so it is a genuinely useful fallback.
The second kind measures amount rather than substance, and this is the group that matters in writing about money.
A great deal of. A large amount of. A small proportion of. A significant quantity of. A fraction of.
And here is the rule that governs them, which you already half know from Level 1 Unit 4.
Amount, quantity and deal go with uncountable nouns. A great deal of money. A large amount of time. A significant quantity of stock.
Number goes with countable ones. A number of items. A large number of complaints.
So it is a large amount of money and a large number of invoices, and swapping them is one of the most visible errors in written English.
The test is the same as in Level 1: can you count it? Money is uncountable — you cannot have three moneys. Invoices are countable.
Second pattern: the language of price, value and contract.
There are three ideas here that learners often merge, and they are different.
Price is what is asked. Cost is what is paid, including everything. Value is what it is worth to you. A low price can be a high cost, if it fails and has to be replaced, and that sentence is the whole of purchasing in one line.
Then the transaction vocabulary. An invoice is a request for payment. A quotation is a fixed price offered in advance. An estimate is an approximation and is not binding. That distinction matters practically: if you accept a quotation the price is fixed, and if you accept an estimate it is not.
Then the contract vocabulary. Terms are the conditions. A clause is one numbered part. Liability is who is responsible when something goes wrong. A warranty is a promise to repair or replace within a period. Void means it no longer applies. Binding means it does.
And one thing worth knowing about how contracts are written: the important clause is almost never the one about what you get. It is the one about what happens when you do not. Level 1 Unit 17 taught you to read to the end of a sign, and the same instinct applies here — the exception is where the money is.
Third pattern, and this is the one that decides outcomes: making a complaint that gets a remedy.
Most complaints fail, and they fail in a predictable way. They describe the problem at length, express dissatisfaction, and never say what they want.
A complaint that works has five parts, and they go in this order.
The facts. What was bought or agreed, when, and what reference it has. Dates and numbers, not adjectives.
The problem. What is wrong, stated plainly and specifically. Not it was terrible — the unit failed after nine days.
The entitlement. Why you are owed something. This is where you name the clause, the warranty, or the statutory right. You do not have to be a lawyer; naming the document is usually enough.
The remedy. What you actually want. This is the part everybody leaves out, and without it the recipient has nothing to agree to.
And the deadline. By when. A complaint with no date can be left indefinitely without anybody having done anything wrong.
Five parts, and the two that decide the outcome are the remedy and the deadline.
Let me be specific about the remedy, because it is where people are vaguest. A remedy is one of a small number of things: a repair, a replacement, a refund, a partial refund, compensation for a consequence, or a written commitment about the future. Choose one. Asking for the problem to be sorted out is not a remedy — it is a mood.
And about tone, which connects to Unit 7. A complaint that is angry is easier to refuse than one that is calm, because anger gives the recipient something to respond to other than the facts. The most effective complaints read as though the writer expects to be dealt with reasonably, and they state the facts, the entitlement, the remedy and the date without adjectives.
One last thing: escalation. If the first response is inadequate, the next step is not a stronger version of the same complaint. It is the same complaint, unchanged, sent to a named person one level up, with the previous correspondence attached and the original deadline restated. Repetition without escalation is what most people do, and it is why most complaints stop.
Go to Patterns.

words.meaning: A part of a larger amount.
words.example: A significant portion of the order was damaged.
practice: Only a small portion is usable.
A portion of the cost is recoverable.
words.starter: A significant portion of the order was
words.tutor: Say a portion of and a proportion of. They overlap and are not identical.

words.meaning: A group of things made or dealt with at one time.
words.example: The whole batch was defective.
practice: It came from the March batch.
The batch number is on the label.
words.starter: The whole batch was
words.tutor: Say the batch number. It is the first thing anybody will ask for in a complaint.

words.meaning: A number of things tied or grouped together.
words.example: It arrived as a bundle of six.
practice: They sell it as a bundle.
words.starter: It arrived as a bundle of
words.tutor: Say bundle as a group of things and as a way of pricing. Both are common.

words.meaning: An amount of something.
words.example: A significant quantity of stock was affected.
practice: The quantity is wrong on the invoice.
In large quantities it is cheaper.
words.starter: A significant quantity of stock was
words.tutor: Quantity goes with uncountable nouns. Say a quantity of stock and a number of items.

words.meaning: A part considered in relation to the whole.
words.example: A large proportion of the batch failed.
words.starter: A large proportion of the batch
words.tutor: Say what proportion is affected. It is a more precise question than how much.

words.meaning: A very small part of something.
words.example: Only a fraction of the cost was refunded.
practice: A fraction of what was promised.
It took a fraction of the time.
words.starter: Only a fraction of the cost was
words.tutor: Fraction implies a very small part. Say fraction and proportion about the same amount.

words.meaning: A document requesting payment for goods or work.
words.example: The invoice does not match the quotation.
practice: I have not received an invoice.
The invoice number is at the top.
Two invoices for the same job.
words.starter: The invoice does not match the
words.tutor: Say the invoice number and date. Both belong in the first line of a complaint.

words.meaning: One of a series of payments.
words.example: It is payable in three instalments.
practice: The first instalment is due on signing.
The final instalment was never taken.
words.starter: It is payable in three
words.tutor: Say payable in instalments. It is the standard phrase in an agreement.

words.meaning: An extra charge added to the basic price.
words.example: There is a surcharge for delivery outside the area.
practice: A ten per cent surcharge applies.
The surcharge appears on the invoice only.
words.starter: There is a surcharge for delivery outside the
words.tutor: Ask whether any surcharge applies. It is a question worth asking before agreeing.

words.meaning: The amount added to the cost to reach the selling price.
words.example: The markup on parts is about forty per cent.
practice: Markup and margin are not the same.
words.starter: The markup on parts is about forty per
words.tutor: Say markup and margin. They measure the same gap from different ends.

words.meaning: The difference between cost and selling price, as a share of the price.
words.example: The margin on this line is very thin.
practice: A thin margin means no room for error.
words.starter: The margin on this line is very
words.tutor: Say a thin margin. It is the standard collocation.

words.meaning: An extra amount paid; or a regular insurance payment.
words.example: You pay a premium for next-day delivery.
practice: A small premium is worth it.
The premium has gone up again.
words.starter: You pay a premium for next-day
words.tutor: Premium means both an extra amount and an insurance payment. Say one sentence with each.

words.meaning: One numbered part of a contract.
words.example: Clause 7 is the one that matters here.
words.starter: Clause 7 is the one that matters
words.tutor: Say name the clause. Citing a number is what makes a complaint hard to dismiss.

words.meaning: The conditions of an agreement. Usually plural.
words.example: The terms have not been met.
practice: Under the terms of the agreement.
I did not accept those terms.
words.starter: The terms have not been
words.tutor: Say under the terms of. It is the standard opening for a contractual claim.

words.meaning: Legal responsibility when something goes wrong.
words.example: Liability is limited to the purchase price.
practice: They accept no liability for delay.
words.starter: Liability is limited to the purchase
words.tutor: Find the liability clause in any contract. It says what you can actually recover.

words.meaning: A written promise to repair or replace within a period.
words.example: It failed within the warranty period.
practice: The warranty does not cover misuse.
words.starter: It failed within the warranty
words.tutor: Say it is still under warranty. That sentence often decides who pays.

words.meaning: No longer valid or in force.
words.example: Opening the unit makes the warranty void.
practice: It becomes void after thirty days.
words.starter: Opening the unit makes the warranty
words.tutor: Say void and expired. One was cancelled; one simply ran out.

words.meaning: Legally enforceable.
words.example: A quotation is binding; an estimate is not.
practice: The agreement is binding on both sides.
words.starter: A quotation is binding; an estimate is
words.tutor: Say the whole example sentence. It is the most useful fact in this group.

words.meaning: Faulty; not working as it should.
words.example: The unit was defective when it arrived.
practice: Two items in the batch were defective.
It is defective rather than damaged.
words.starter: The unit was defective when it
words.tutor: Say defective and damaged. One was made wrong; one was harmed afterwards.

words.meaning: Below the required or expected quality.
words.example: The work was substandard rather than unfinished.
practice: It is substandard by any measure.
words.starter: The work was substandard rather than
words.tutor: Say substandard. It is more specific and harder to argue with than bad.

words.meaning: To charge more than the correct amount.
words.example: We were overcharged by about eighty pounds.
words.starter: We were overcharged by about eighty
words.tutor: Notice the number. Overcharged by an amount is a claim; overcharged alone is a feeling.

words.meaning: A difference between two things that should match.
words.example: There is a discrepancy between the invoice and the quotation.
practice: The discrepancy is about forty pounds.
The discrepancy has not been explained.
words.starter: There is a discrepancy between the invoice and the
words.tutor: Say a discrepancy between two things. It is neutral and it names a fact.

words.meaning: A formal complaint, especially at work.
words.example: She raised a grievance in March.
words.starter: She raised a grievance in
words.tutor: Grievance is the workplace word. Say raised a grievance and made a complaint.

words.meaning: Putting right something that was wrong.
words.example: What redress is available?
practice: There is no redress under this clause.
words.starter: What redress is
words.tutor: Say redress rather than apology. That is the whole point of card 3.

words.meaning: Money paid for loss or inconvenience caused.
words.example: I am seeking compensation for the two days lost.
practice: Compensation of about two hundred pounds.
Compensation is not the same as a refund.
words.starter: I am seeking compensation for the two days
words.tutor: Say compensation for a named loss. Compensation without a loss attached is refused.

words.meaning: A new item given in place of a faulty one.
words.example: I would like a replacement rather than a repair.
practice: The replacement arrived damaged as well.
words.starter: I would like a replacement rather than a
words.tutor: Say replacement, refund or repair. Naming which one you want is what makes it a remedy.

words.meaning: To pay somebody back money they have spent.
words.example: Please reimburse the hire cost of eighty pounds.
practice: They agreed to reimburse the difference.
words.starter: Please reimburse the hire cost of eighty
words.tutor: Say please reimburse a named amount. Vagueness here is why complaints fail.

words.meaning: To take a complaint to a higher level.
words.example: I will escalate it if I have no reply by Friday.
practice: It was escalated to the regional manager.
words.starter: I will escalate it if I have no reply by
words.tutor: Say escalate rather than repeat. Sending the same complaint again is not escalation.

words.meaning: An independent official who investigates complaints against organisations.
words.example: The ombudsman only takes a case after eight weeks.
practice: I referred it to the ombudsman.
The ombudsman found in my favour.
There is an ombudsman for this sector.
The ombudsman is free to use.
words.starter: The ombudsman only takes a case after eight
words.tutor: Find out whether your sector has an ombudsman. It is the last step and it costs nothing.

readings.title: Amount or Number
readings.passage:
English measures uncountable things with special expressions, and Level 1 Unit 6 gave you the physical ones — a packet of, a bottle of, a slice of. Those are learned with the substance and there is no rule behind them. A grain of rice, a sheet of paper, a bar of soap.
When you do not know the right one, use piece. A piece of paper, a piece of equipment, a piece of advice, a piece of information. Piece works for almost anything and never sounds wrong, which makes it a genuinely useful fallback rather than a compromise.
The second group measures amount rather than substance, and it is the one that matters in writing about money.
A great deal of. A large amount of. A significant quantity of. A small proportion of. A fraction of. A number of.
The rule that governs them is one you half know already from Level 1 Unit 4.
Amount, quantity and deal go with uncountable nouns.
A great deal of money. A large amount of time. A significant quantity of stock.
Number goes with countable nouns.
A number of items. A large number of complaints. A small number of invoices.
So it is a large amount of money and a large number of invoices, and swapping them is one of the most visible errors in written English — visible because it appears in the sort of writing where people are paying attention.
The test is the same as it was in Level 1. Can you count it? You cannot have three moneys or four stocks, so those take amount. You can have three invoices, so they take number.
One group is genuinely awkward and worth naming. Some words are countable in one sense and uncountable in another. Time is uncountable when it means duration — a great deal of time — and countable when it means occasions — a number of times. Both are correct and they mean different things, so the rule still holds; you just have to notice which sense you are in.

readings.title: The Complaint That Gets Paid
readings.passage:
Most complaints fail, and they fail in a predictable way. They describe the problem at length, express how the writer feels about it, and never say what they want.
A complaint that works has five parts, in this order.
The facts. What was bought or agreed, when, and the reference number. Dates and figures, not adjectives.
The problem. What is wrong, plainly and specifically. Not the service was terrible, but the unit failed after nine days.
The entitlement. Why you are owed something — the clause, the warranty, the terms. You do not have to argue law; naming the document is usually enough to show you have read it.
The remedy. What you actually want.
The deadline. By when.
The last two decide the outcome, and the remedy is the one people are vaguest about.
A remedy is one of a small number of things: a repair, a replacement, a refund, a partial refund, reimbursement of a specific cost you incurred, compensation for a named consequence, or a written commitment about the future.
Choose one and name it. Asking for the matter to be sorted out is not a remedy — it is a mood, and there is nothing for the recipient to agree to.
The deadline matters for a reason that is easy to miss. A complaint with no date can be left indefinitely, and nobody has done anything wrong. A complaint with a date converts silence into a fact you can point to later.
Then there is tone, and it connects directly to Unit 7.
An angry complaint is easier to refuse than a calm one, because anger gives the recipient something to respond to other than the facts. If they can reply to your tone, they never have to reply to your claim.
The most effective complaints read as though the writer expects to be dealt with reasonably. They state the facts, the entitlement, the remedy and the date, and they use almost no adjectives.
Finally, escalation, which almost everybody gets wrong.
If the first reply is inadequate, the next step is not a stronger version of the same complaint. It is the same complaint, unchanged, sent to a named person one level up, with the previous correspondence attached and the deadline restated.
Repetition is not escalation, and repetition is what most people do. It is the single commonest reason a legitimate complaint stops.

readings.title: One Problem, Two Letters
readings.setting: Two customers wrote about the same faulty batch. One was paid and one was not.
readings.passage:
LETTER A

  I am writing to complain about the
  appalling service I have received. The
  unit I bought from you has been nothing
  but trouble since the day it arrived and
  frankly I am disgusted.

  I have telephoned three times and each
  time I have been passed around and
  nobody has any idea what is going on.
  This is completely unacceptable and I
  have wasted hours of my time.

  I would like this sorted out as soon as
  possible. I have been a customer for
  years and I expect better.

  OUTCOME: apology sent. No further
  action.

-----------------------------------------

  LETTER B

  Order 44192, placed 2 February,
  invoice dated 9 February.

  The unit (batch 0219-C) stopped working
  on 18 February, nine days after
  delivery. It has not restarted. I
  reported this by telephone on 18 and 21
  February, reference CS-8841.

  Clause 6.2 of your terms provides a
  twelve-month warranty covering failure
  not caused by misuse. The unit has been
  used only as described in your own
  instructions.

  I am asking for two things: a
  replacement unit, and reimbursement of
  the 80 hire charge I incurred between
  19 and 26 February, receipt attached.

  Please confirm both by 14 March. If I
  have not heard by then I will write to
  your Head of Customer Operations and
  attach this correspondence.

  OUTCOME: replacement sent 11 March,
  hire charge reimbursed.

comprehension.q: What is the rule for amount and number?
comprehension.a: Amount, quantity and deal go with uncountable nouns; number goes with countable ones. A large amount of money, a large number of invoices.
comprehension.why: It is the same countability test as Level 1 Unit 4, applied to a new set of expressions.

comprehension.q: What does the text recommend when you do not know the right partitive?
comprehension.a: Use piece — a piece of paper, a piece of equipment, a piece of advice. It works for almost anything and never sounds wrong.
comprehension.why: A reliable fallback is more useful than an incomplete list, because the physical partitives have no rule behind them.

comprehension.q: Why is time an awkward case?
comprehension.a: It is uncountable when it means duration — a great deal of time — and countable when it means occasions — a number of times. Both are correct and they mean different things.
comprehension.why: The rule still holds; the difficulty is noticing which sense you are in, which is worth naming rather than treating as an exception.

comprehension.q: What are the five parts of a complaint that works?
comprehension.a: The facts, the problem, the entitlement, the remedy, and the deadline.
comprehension.why: They go in that order, and the last two are the ones that decide whether anything happens.

comprehension.q: Why is asking for the matter to be sorted out not a remedy?
comprehension.a: Because it is a mood rather than a request — there is nothing specific for the recipient to agree to.
comprehension.why: This is the part people are vaguest about, and it is the single most common reason a legitimate complaint produces nothing.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say an angry complaint is easier to refuse?
comprehension.a: Because anger gives the recipient something to respond to other than the facts. If they can reply to your tone, they never have to reply to your claim.
comprehension.why: It reframes calm not as politeness but as tactics, which is a more persuasive argument for it.

comprehension.q: Letter A describes a real problem and gets nothing. What is missing?
comprehension.a: Everything checkable. There are no dates, no order or reference numbers, no statement of what is actually wrong with the unit, no entitlement, no specific remedy and no deadline.
comprehension.why: The problem is real and the letter gives the recipient nothing to act on, which is why an apology is a complete response to it.

comprehension.q: List the checkable facts in Letter B.
comprehension.a: Order 44192, placed 2 February, invoice 9 February, batch 0219-C, failed 18 February, nine days after delivery, reported 18 and 21 February, reference CS-8841, clause 6.2, twelve-month warranty, 80 hire charge, 19 to 26 February, receipt attached, deadline 14 March.
comprehension.why: Fourteen checkable items in four short paragraphs. Every one of them can be verified by the recipient without asking the writer anything.

comprehension.q: Letter B asks for two things. What are they, and why is the second one harder to refuse than a general request for compensation?
comprehension.a: A replacement unit, and reimbursement of the 80 hire charge. The second is a specific sum, for a named period, caused by the fault, with a receipt attached — so refusing it requires disputing a documented cost rather than declining a vague claim.
comprehension.why: Compensation for a named and evidenced consequence is a different kind of request from compensation for inconvenience.

comprehension.q: What does Letter B's final sentence do?
comprehension.a: It sets a deadline and states the escalation in advance — a named role one level up, with the correspondence attached. It converts silence into a consequence.
comprehension.why: Naming the escalation before it is needed is what makes the deadline real, and it does so without any threat or change of tone.

grammar.title: Partitive expressions
grammar.explanation: The words English uses to measure things you cannot count. There are two groups: one for physical substances, and one for amount — and only the second has a rule.
grammar.rule:
GROUP 1 - PHYSICAL. No rule.
  a grain of rice   a sheet of paper
  a bar of soap     a strip of tape
  a drop of water   a length of cable
  a batch of units  a bundle of forms

  learned with the substance.

  WHEN YOU DO NOT KNOW ONE, USE PIECE
     a piece of paper / equipment /
     advice / information / news
  ^ works for almost anything.

GROUP 2 - AMOUNT. This one HAS a rule.

  UNCOUNTABLE -> amount, quantity, deal
     a large amount of money
     a great deal of time
     a significant quantity of stock

  COUNTABLE -> number
     a number of items
     a large number of complaints

  THE TEST: can you count it?
     three moneys? no  -> amount
     three invoices? yes -> number

THE AWKWARD ONES
  time = duration -> a great deal of time
  time = occasions -> a number of times
  Both correct. Notice which sense.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to say that a lot of money was involved.
1. Is money countable? Try it: one money, two moneys. No.
2. Uncountable takes amount, quantity or deal.
3. Result: a large amount of money, or a great deal of money.
Now the other side. You want to say that a lot of invoices were affected.
1. Is invoice countable? One invoice, two invoices. Yes.
2. Countable takes number.
3. Result: a large number of invoices.
And a physical one you do not know. You want to name a single unit of paper.
1. Is there a specific partitive? Yes — a sheet of paper.
2. If you did not know it, the fallback would work: a piece of paper. Both are correct and one required no knowledge.
That fallback is why this card does not need a longer list. Piece covers what you do not know, and the amount rule covers what matters in writing.
grammar.mistake: Swapping amount and number — a large number of money, a large amount of invoices. It is highly visible because it appears in the kind of writing where readers are paying attention. The other error is over-using the physical partitives when piece would do; a piece of equipment is always safe and an invented partitive is not.
grammar.tip: Uncountable takes amount. Countable takes number. Unsure of a partitive? Piece.
grammar.practice:
Write amount or number, and say why.
1. a large ____ of money
2. a large ____ of invoices
3. a great ____ of time
4. a small ____ of complaints
5. a significant ____ of stock
6. a ____ of times (meaning occasions)
grammar.answers:
1. amount — money is uncountable.
2. number — invoices are countable.
3. deal — time as duration is uncountable. Amount also works.
4. number — complaints are countable.
5. quantity — stock is uncountable. Amount also works.
6. number — times meaning occasions is countable.
Numbers 3 and 6 are the same word in two senses. Duration takes deal or amount; occasions take number. The rule did not change — the noun did.
If you were unsure about stock in 5, apply the test: one stock, two stocks does not work in this sense, so it is uncountable.

grammar.title: Price, value and contract
grammar.explanation: Three ideas that learners merge, and the transaction vocabulary that depends on keeping them apart. Most of this is precision rather than grammar, and the precision is worth money.
grammar.rule:
THREE DIFFERENT THINGS
  PRICE  what is ASKED
  COST   what is PAID, all in
  VALUE  what it is WORTH to you

  "A low price can be a high cost."
  ^ if it fails and must be replaced.

THE TRANSACTION WORDS
  INVOICE     a request for payment
  QUOTATION   a FIXED price, offered
              in advance
  ESTIMATE    an approximation.
              NOT binding.

  Accept a quotation -> price is fixed.
  Accept an estimate -> it is not.

THE CONTRACT WORDS
  TERMS      the conditions
  CLAUSE     one numbered part
  LIABILITY  who is responsible when it
             goes wrong
  WARRANTY   a promise to repair or
             replace within a period
  VOID       no longer applies
  BINDING    it does apply

WHERE THE MONEY IS
  the important clause is rarely the one
  about what you GET. It is the one about
  what happens when you DON'T.
  (Level 1 Unit 17: read to the end.)
grammar.workedExample:
Somebody offers to do a job and sends you a figure. Before agreeing, you want to know what you are committing to.
1. Ask which it is: a quotation or an estimate.
2. If it is a quotation, the price is fixed and accepting it binds both sides.
3. If it is an estimate, it is an approximation and the final invoice may differ.
4. That single question is the difference between knowing what you will pay and not.
Now the price-and-cost distinction. Two units are offered, one cheaper.
1. Price: the cheaper one is 200 and the other is 320.
2. Cost: the cheaper one has a one-year warranty and the other has three. If the cheap one fails in year two you buy another, so the cost over three years is 400 against 320.
3. Value: what it is worth to you depends on how long you need it. If you need it for one year, the cheap one is better on all three measures.
Price is a number on a page. Cost is what leaves your account. Value is a judgement, and only the third one depends on you.
grammar.mistake: Treating an estimate as a fixed price, which is the commonest and most expensive confusion in this area. The other error is reading a contract for what you get rather than for what happens when something fails — the liability clause and the warranty exclusions are where the money is, and they are almost never in the first paragraph.
grammar.tip: Price is asked, cost is paid, value is worth. Quotations bind; estimates do not.
grammar.practice:
Answer each in a full sentence.
1. What is the difference between price and cost?
2. What is the difference between a quotation and an estimate?
3. What does void mean, and how does it differ from expired?
4. What does a liability clause tell you?
5. Which part of a warranty matters most, and why?
6. Give an example of a low price that is a high cost.
grammar.answers:
1. Price is what is asked; cost is what is actually paid, including everything that follows.
2. A quotation is a fixed price and is binding once accepted. An estimate is an approximation and is not.
3. Void means it has been cancelled and no longer applies — often because a condition was broken. Expired means it simply ran out of time.
4. It tells you who is responsible when something goes wrong, and usually how much can be recovered.
5. The exclusions — what the warranty does not cover. The promise is easy to find; the exceptions are where claims fail.
6. Model: a unit at 200 with a one-year warranty against one at 320 with three years. If the first fails in year two, three years cost 400 rather than 320.
Number 5 is the point worth carrying beyond this unit. In any document that offers you something, the exception is where the money is.

grammar.title: A complaint that gets a remedy
grammar.explanation: Five parts in a fixed order. The last two decide the outcome, and the remedy is the one almost everybody leaves out.
grammar.rule:
FIVE PARTS, IN THIS ORDER

  1 THE FACTS
     what, when, reference number.
     Dates and figures, not adjectives.
  2 THE PROBLEM
     plainly and specifically.
     not \"terrible\" - \"failed after 9 days\"
  3 THE ENTITLEMENT
     the clause, warranty or terms.
     Naming the document is usually enough.
  4 THE REMEDY
     what you actually WANT.
  5 THE DEADLINE
     by when.

A REMEDY IS ONE OF THESE
  a repair / a replacement / a refund /
  a partial refund / reimbursement of a
  named cost / compensation for a named
  consequence / a written commitment

  \"Please sort this out\" is NOT a remedy.
  It is a mood.

TONE (see Unit 7)
  an ANGRY complaint is EASIER to refuse -
  they can answer your tone instead of
  your claim.

ESCALATION
  NOT a stronger version of the same
  letter. The SAME letter, to a NAMED
  person one level up, with the previous
  correspondence attached.
grammar.workedExample:
A unit you bought failed nine days after delivery and you hired a replacement while waiting.
1. Facts. Order number, order date, invoice date, batch number. No adjectives at all.
2. Problem. The unit stopped working on 18 February, nine days after delivery, and has not restarted. Specific and dated.
3. Entitlement. Clause 6.2 provides a twelve-month warranty covering failure not caused by misuse, and the unit has been used only as described in your own instructions. That last clause closes the obvious refusal.
4. Remedy. Two things, both named: a replacement unit, and reimbursement of the 80 hire charge with the receipt attached.
5. Deadline. Please confirm both by 14 March. And the escalation, stated in advance: if I have not heard, I will write to your Head of Customer Operations and attach this correspondence.
Notice what is not there: no adjectives, no account of how many times you telephoned unless it is a dated fact, and no statement of how you feel.
The letter is short, entirely checkable, and there is nothing in it to reply to except the request.
grammar.mistake: Describing the problem at length and never saying what you want, which is what almost all failed complaints do. An apology is a complete response to a letter that asks for nothing. The other error is escalating by rewriting the same complaint more angrily; escalation means the same complaint to a higher named person, and repetition is not escalation.
grammar.tip: Facts, problem, entitlement, remedy, deadline. Name the remedy.
grammar.practice:
Answer each in a full sentence.
1. What are the five parts, in order?
2. Why is please sort this out not a remedy?
3. Name four things that are remedies.
4. Why does a deadline matter?
5. Why is an angry complaint easier to refuse?
6. What is the correct next step if the first reply is inadequate?
grammar.answers:
1. The facts, the problem, the entitlement, the remedy, and the deadline.
2. Because there is nothing specific to agree to. It expresses dissatisfaction rather than making a request, so an apology answers it completely.
3. A replacement, a refund, reimbursement of a named cost, and compensation for a named consequence. A repair, a partial refund and a written commitment also count.
4. Because without one the complaint can be left indefinitely and nobody has done anything wrong. A date converts silence into a fact you can point to.
5. Because anger gives the recipient something to answer other than the facts. If they can respond to your tone, they never have to respond to your claim.
6. Send the same complaint, unchanged, to a named person one level up, with the previous correspondence attached and the deadline restated.
Number 6 is the one most people get wrong. Repetition is not escalation, and it is the commonest reason a legitimate complaint stops.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Amount or number
speaking.instructions:
Say twelve phrases aloud, six with amount or quantity and six with number.
A large amount of money. A large number of invoices.
Before each one, say aloud whether the noun is countable, and how you know.
Record all twelve.
The test is the same every time: can you say two of them?
speaking.tutor: Say twelve nouns and ask the tutor whether each takes amount or number.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Price, cost, value
speaking.instructions:
Take four things you have bought or would buy.
For each, say three sentences: its price, its cost including everything that followed, and its value to you.
Record all twelve.
Then say one example of a low price that turned out to be a high cost. Almost everybody has one, and saying it aloud fixes the distinction better than the definition does.
speaking.tutor: Describe a purchase to the tutor and ask it to distinguish the price, the cost and the value.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — The five parts
speaking.instructions:
Take a real problem you have had with something bought or arranged.
Say the five parts aloud, one sentence each: facts, problem, entitlement, remedy, deadline.
Do this for three different problems.
Record all fifteen sentences.
Check the remedy sentence in each. If it does not name a repair, replacement, refund, reimbursement or written commitment, it is not a remedy.
speaking.tutor: Describe a problem to the tutor and ask it to identify which of the five parts you left out.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Ask for it on the telephone
speaking.instructions:
Say both sides, then change the problem three times.
A: I'm calling about order 44192. The unit failed on the eighteenth, nine days after delivery.
B: I'll pass you to the technical team.
A: Before you do — I'd like to be clear about what I'm asking for. Under clause 6.2 it's within warranty, so I'm asking for a replacement and reimbursement of the hire cost, which is eighty pounds and I have the receipt. Can you note that on the file?
B: I'll add it.
A: Thank you. Could I have a reference for this call, and could you tell me by when I'll have an answer?
Notice A named the remedy before being transferred, and asked for a reference and a date.
Record one full version.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to be a call handler who tries to pass you on, and state your remedy before it does.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Say it without adjectives
speaking.instructions:
Take four things that have genuinely annoyed you about a product or service.
Describe each one twice: once as you would naturally, and once with no adjectives at all — only facts, dates and numbers.
Record all eight.
Listen back to each pair. The version without adjectives is shorter and harder to dismiss, and that is the whole argument of card 3.
speaking.tutor: Describe a problem to the tutor with no adjectives and ask what it now knows.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read both letters aloud
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read Letter A aloud, then Letter B.
Then say aloud: what Letter A is missing, given that the problem in it is real.
Then count the checkable facts in Letter B aloud.
Then say what B's final sentence does and why it works without any threat in it.
Record the last three parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Read the tutor Letter A and ask what it would do if it received it.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A complaint in five parts
writing.prompt:
Write a complaint about something real or invented — a faulty item, a service that was not delivered, an incorrect charge.
Use all five parts, clearly separated.
The facts paragraph must contain at least four checkable items: dates, reference numbers, amounts.
The problem must be stated with no adjectives at all.
The entitlement must name a clause, a warranty or a stated term.
The remedy must name at least one specific thing.
The deadline must be a date, and the escalation must be stated in advance.
writing.model:
Order 51108, placed 14 April, invoice 51108-A dated 16 April, delivered 21 April.

The heater (model TC-40, serial 9930221) stopped producing heat on 2 May, eleven days after delivery. It has not restarted. I reported this by telephone on 2 and 6 May, reference HS-2214, and by email on 6 May.

Clause 8.1 of your published terms provides a two-year warranty covering component failure. Clause 8.3 excludes damage caused by misuse; the unit has been used only in the manner set out in your installation guide, and it was installed by your own engineer on 21 April.

I am asking for two things: a replacement unit of the same model, and reimbursement of the 64 I paid to hire a heater between 3 and 12 May. The hire receipt is attached.

Please confirm both in writing by 30 May. If I have not received a reply by that date I will write to your Head of Customer Operations, attaching this letter and the previous correspondence.
writing.criteria: At least four checkable items in the facts; a problem stated with no adjectives; an entitlement naming a specific clause, warranty or term; at least one named remedy; a dated deadline; the escalation stated in advance; no statement of how the writer feels anywhere in the letter
writing.support: Write the remedy first, at the bottom of the page, then build everything above it. A complaint written forwards tends to arrive at no request at all, which is exactly how most of them fail.
writing.extension: Count the adjectives in your finished letter. A good one has almost none, and the ones it has are factual — faulty, incorrect, outstanding.

writing.title: Writing 2 — The escalation
writing.prompt:
Take your complaint from Writing 1.
Invent an inadequate reply to it — an apology with no remedy, or a partial offer.
Then write the escalation.
It must be the same complaint, not an angrier one. It must go to a named role one level up. It must attach the previous correspondence, restate the original remedy unchanged, and set a new date.
Then write three lines: what you changed from the original, what you deliberately did not change, and what the reply would have had to contain to make escalation unnecessary.
writing.model:
THE REPLY RECEIVED
"Thank you for contacting us. We are sorry to hear of the difficulty you have experienced with your heater. Our engineers advise that a service visit may resolve the issue and we have passed your details to the scheduling team, who will be in touch within 28 days. We value your custom."

THE ESCALATION
For the attention of the Head of Customer Operations.
I wrote on 12 May about order 51108 (heater TC-40, serial 9930221), which failed on 2 May, eleven days after delivery. Copies of that letter and of your reply of 19 May are attached.
Your reply offers a service visit within 28 days. It does not address either of the two things I asked for.
Under clause 8.1 the unit is within a two-year warranty for component failure. Clause 8.3 does not apply: the unit was installed by your own engineer on 21 April and used as set out in your guide.
I am asking for the same two things: a replacement unit of the same model, and reimbursement of the 64 hire charge incurred between 3 and 12 May. The receipt was attached to my original letter and is attached again.
Please confirm both in writing by 6 June.

1. I changed the addressee, added the reference to the previous correspondence, added one sentence saying what the reply did not address, and set a new date.
2. I did not change the remedy, the entitlement, the facts, or the tone. The request is word for word what it was.
3. The reply would have had to do one of two things: agree to both requests, or refuse one of them with a reason under a named clause. An offer of a service visit does neither — it answers a complaint I did not make.
writing.length: An invented reply plus the escalation plus three lines
writing.criteria: The escalation addresses a named role one level up; the remedy is restated unchanged; the previous correspondence is referenced as attached; one sentence identifies what the reply failed to address; a new deadline is set; the tone is identical to the original; three lines of commentary
writing.support: Put the two letters side by side when you finish. If more than four things differ, you have rewritten the complaint rather than escalated it.
writing.extension: Write the version most people would actually send — the same complaint, angrier. Then say what a recipient could reply to in that version that they could not in yours.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the two letters
writing.prompt:
Use the two letters in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. The problem in Letter A is real. Why does an apology answer it completely?
2. List eight checkable facts in Letter B.
3. Letter B asks for two things. Why is the second harder to refuse than a general request for compensation?
4. What does B's final sentence achieve, and why does it work without any threat?
5. Rewrite Letter A as a complaint that would have been paid, inventing plausible detail.
writing.model:
1. Because the letter asks for nothing. It describes dissatisfaction and requests that the matter be sorted out, so an expression of regret is a complete and reasonable response to it. There is no specific claim to accept or refuse.
2. Order 44192; placed 2 February; invoice dated 9 February; batch 0219-C; failure on 18 February; nine days after delivery; telephone reports on 18 and 21 February; reference CS-8841; clause 6.2; twelve-month warranty; hire charge of 80; period 19 to 26 February; receipt attached; deadline 14 March. Any eight.
3. Because it is a specific sum, for a named period, caused by the fault, with a receipt attached. Refusing it means disputing a documented cost rather than declining a general claim about inconvenience, which is a much harder thing to do in writing.
4. It sets a deadline and names the escalation in advance — a specific role, with the correspondence attached. It works without a threat because it states what the writer will do rather than what will happen to the recipient, and because it is entirely proportionate.
5. Model: Order 33871, placed 3 March, invoice 33871-B dated 5 March, delivered 8 March. The unit stopped working on 17 March, nine days after delivery, and has not restarted. I reported it by telephone on 17, 19 and 24 March; I was not given a reference on any of those calls, which is why I am writing. Clause 6.2 of your terms provides a twelve-month warranty for failure not caused by misuse. I am asking for a replacement unit, and for confirmation of the reference number for my three earlier calls. Please confirm both by 8 April; if I have not heard I will write to your Head of Customer Operations attaching this letter.
writing.starter: 1. Because the letter asks for nothing.
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 2 lists eight genuine checkable items; answer 3 explains the difference between a documented cost and a general claim; answer 5 supplies all five parts and turns A's complaint about being passed around into a checkable fact
writing.support: For question 5, notice that A's real grievance — three phone calls and nobody knowing anything — can become a checkable fact rather than a complaint about feelings. Dates of calls, and the absence of a reference number, are both verifiable.
writing.extension: Count the adjectives in each letter. A has about ten and B has almost none, and that count tracks the outcome exactly.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the twelve
writing.prompt:
Every item has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. a large number of money
2. a large amount of invoices
3. a great deal of complaints
4. a significant number of stock
5. I accepted the estimate, so the price is fixed.
6. The warranty expired because I opened the unit.
7. The price of the cheap one was lower, so it cost less. (it failed in year two)
8. I would like this sorted out as soon as possible. (as the remedy)
9. I am disgusted by the service I have received. (in a complaint)
10. Please reply soon. (as the deadline)
11. I am writing again to complain in the strongest possible terms. (as the escalation)
12. I would like compensation. (with no consequence named)
writing.model:
1. a large amount of money (Pattern 1 — money is uncountable)
2. a large number of invoices (Pattern 1 — invoices are countable)
3. a great number of complaints (Pattern 1 — complaints are countable; or a great deal of complaint, uncountable, meaning dissatisfaction)
4. a significant quantity of stock (Pattern 1 — stock is uncountable)
5. I accepted the quotation, so the price is fixed. (Pattern 2 — an estimate is not binding)
6. The warranty is void because I opened the unit. (Pattern 2 — void means cancelled by a breach; expired means it ran out)
7. The price was lower but the cost was higher. (Pattern 2 — price is asked, cost is what is actually paid)
8. I am asking for a replacement unit and reimbursement of the 80 hire charge. (Pattern 3 — name the remedy)
9. The unit failed on 18 February, nine days after delivery. (Pattern 3 — facts, not feelings)
10. Please confirm by 14 March. (Pattern 3 — a deadline is a date)
11. Send the same complaint, unchanged, to a named person one level up with the correspondence attached. (Pattern 3 — repetition is not escalation)
12. I am asking for reimbursement of the 80 hire charge I incurred between 19 and 26 February. (Pattern 3 — compensation needs a named and evidenced consequence)
writing.criteria: All twelve corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; numbers 1 to 4 all decided by countability; numbers 8 to 12 all fixed by adding specificity rather than force
writing.support: Numbers 8 to 12 all fail the same way: they express feeling or urgency where a specific request belongs. For each, ask what exactly you want the recipient to do, and write that instead.
writing.extension: Number 11 is the escalation error and it is the commonest of the twelve in real life. Write the correct escalation for any complaint you have actually made.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Amount, number, quantity
activities.instructions:
Write amount, number, quantity or deal, and mark C for countable or U for uncountable.
1. a large ____ of money
2. a large ____ of invoices
3. a great ____ of time
4. a small ____ of complaints
5. a significant ____ of stock
6. a ____ of times (occasions)
7. a large ____ of work
8. a small ____ of items
9. a great ____ of effort
10. a ____ of discrepancies
11. a significant ____ of damage
12. a large ____ of customers
activities.answers:
1. amount — U  2. number — C  3. deal — U  4. number — C  5. quantity — U  6. number — C  7. amount — U  8. number — C  9. deal — U  10. number — C  11. amount — U  12. number — C
The test worked on all twelve: two moneys, two times, two works, two efforts and two damages are all impossible, so those take amount, deal or quantity. Two invoices, two complaints, two items, two discrepancies and two customers are all fine, so those take number.
Numbers 3 and 6 are the same word in different senses. Duration is uncountable and occasions are countable, and the rule handles both correctly once you notice which sense you are in.
Number 11 is worth checking: damage is uncountable in English even though damages exists as a legal term meaning compensation.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Which word?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right word.
1. A document requesting payment is an (invoice / estimate / quotation).
2. A fixed price offered in advance is an (invoice / estimate / quotation).
3. An approximation that is not binding is an (invoice / estimate / quotation).
4. What is asked for something is its (price / cost / value).
5. What you actually end up paying is its (price / cost / value).
6. What it is worth to you is its (price / cost / value).
7. Who is responsible when it goes wrong is covered by the (warranty / liability / margin) clause.
8. A promise to repair or replace within a period is a (warranty / liability / surcharge).
9. No longer valid because a condition was broken: (void / expired / binding).
10. Ran out of time: (void / expired / binding).
11. Legally enforceable: (void / expired / binding).
12. An extra charge added to the basic price is a (margin / surcharge / discrepancy).
activities.answers:
1. invoice  2. quotation  3. estimate  4. price  5. cost  6. value  7. liability  8. warranty  9. void  10. expired  11. binding  12. surcharge
Numbers 2 and 3 are the pair that costs money. Accepting a quotation fixes the price; accepting an estimate does not, and the words look similar enough that the distinction is easy to lose.
Numbers 9 and 10 are also worth separating. Void means cancelled, usually because a condition was broken. Expired means it simply ran out. A warranty voided by opening the unit and a warranty that expired after two years are different situations with different arguments available.
Numbers 4, 5 and 6 are the three that learners merge, and the low-price-high-cost case is where the difference shows.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Is that a remedy?
activities.instructions:
Write REMEDY or NOT. For each NOT, rewrite it as a remedy.
1. Please sort this out as soon as possible.
2. I would like a replacement unit.
3. I expect better.
4. Please reimburse the 80 hire charge, receipt attached.
5. This is completely unacceptable.
6. I am asking for a full refund of the invoice amount.
7. I have wasted hours of my time.
8. I would like written confirmation that the surcharge will not be applied again.
9. Something needs to be done.
10. I am asking for a partial refund of 40, being half the delivery charge.
11. I would like an apology.
12. Please arrange a repair within fourteen days.
activities.answers:
REMEDY: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.
NOT: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11.
Rewrites:
1. I am asking for a replacement unit within fourteen days.
3. I am asking for reimbursement of the hire charge I incurred while waiting.
5. I am asking for a full refund of the invoice amount.
7. I am asking for compensation of 60 for the two days the unit was unavailable.
9. I am asking for a repair by 14 March, or a replacement if a repair is not possible.
11. An apology is not a remedy. I am asking for a written commitment that the surcharge will not be applied to future orders.
Every genuine remedy names a specific thing: a replacement, a named sum, a refund, a written commitment, a repair with a date.
Number 11 is worth a second look. An apology can be requested and it is not a remedy, because it costs nothing and changes nothing. If you want one, ask for it in addition to a remedy rather than instead of one.
Number 7 shows compensation done properly: a named sum, for a named consequence, over a named period.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Find the missing part
activities.instructions:
Each of these complaints is missing one or more of the five parts. Say which are missing and supply them.
1. "Order 44192, invoice 9 February. The unit failed on 18 February. Clause 6.2 provides a twelve-month warranty. Please confirm by 14 March."
2. "The unit failed nine days after delivery. I am asking for a replacement. Please confirm by 14 March."
3. "Order 44192, invoice 9 February. The unit failed on 18 February, nine days after delivery. Clause 6.2 provides a twelve-month warranty. I am asking for a replacement."
4. "I have been a customer for years and the service has been appalling. I would like this looked at."
activities.answers:
1. Missing the REMEDY. Add: I am asking for a replacement unit and reimbursement of the 80 hire charge, receipt attached.
2. Missing the FACTS and the ENTITLEMENT. Add: Order 44192, placed 2 February, invoice dated 9 February, batch 0219-C. And: Clause 6.2 of your terms provides a twelve-month warranty covering failure not caused by misuse.
3. Missing the DEADLINE. Add: Please confirm by 14 March. If I have not heard by then I will write to your Head of Customer Operations attaching this correspondence.
4. Missing all five. There are no facts, the problem is stated only as an adjective, there is no entitlement, looked at is not a remedy, and there is no date.
Number 1 is the commonest real failure — everything is present except the request, and a complaint with no request cannot be granted.
Number 3 is the second commonest. A complete complaint with no deadline can be left indefinitely without anybody having done anything wrong.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Read a real contract clause
activities.instructions:
Find a real set of terms — a warranty, a service agreement, terms and conditions, an insurance policy.
Find three things: the warranty or guarantee clause, the liability clause, and the exclusions.
Write down what each one says in plain English.
Then write one line on what would have to happen for you to recover nothing.
activities.answers:
No key — they are your terms.
What most people find: the promise is easy to find and the exclusions are not. The warranty clause is usually short and prominent, and the list of what it does not cover is longer, later, and written in a denser register.
The second finding is about liability. Most consumer and commercial contracts limit liability to the purchase price, which means that if a failure causes you a larger loss — a day's work, a hire charge, a missed deadline — you may not be able to recover it under the contract even though the failure was theirs.
The third finding is the answer to the last question, and it is worth knowing before you need it: in most terms, you recover nothing if the exclusion applies, if you did not report it within the stated period, or if you did something the terms describe as misuse. Two of those three are entirely within your control, and both are about acting quickly and in writing.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Rewrite a complaint you sent
activities.instructions:
Find a complaint you have actually made — by email, by message, or in a letter.
Mark which of the five parts it contained.
Count the adjectives.
Rewrite it with all five parts and no adjectives in the problem statement.
Write two lines: which part was missing, and whether the reply you received would have been possible if that part had been there.
activities.answers:
No key — it is your complaint.
What almost everybody finds: the missing part is the remedy. The facts are usually there, the problem is described at length, and the letter ends with something like please look into this or I hope you can resolve this.
The second finding is the important one. The reply you received was almost certainly a complete and reasonable answer to the letter you actually sent. That is uncomfortable and it is the most useful thing this task produces — the reply was not evasive; the request was absent.
The third finding is about adjectives. Most people count between six and fifteen in a complaint of a few paragraphs, and almost none of them are load-bearing. Removing them shortens the letter and makes it harder to answer with sympathy instead of action.

quizzes.why: Money is uncountable — you cannot have three moneys — so it takes amount, quantity or deal. Number goes with countable nouns.
Invoices are countable, so they take number. Swapping amount and number is one of the most visible errors in written English.

quizzes.q: You do not know the right partitive for something. What is the safe fallback?
quizzes.why: A piece of paper, a piece of equipment, a piece of advice, a piece of information. It works for almost anything and never sounds wrong.

quizzes.q: What is the difference between a quotation and an estimate?
options: An estimate is fixed and a quotation is not
A quotation is fixed and binding; an estimate is not
A quotation is verbal and an estimate is written
quizzes.a: A quotation is fixed and binding; an estimate is not
quizzes.why: Accepting a quotation fixes the price. Accepting an estimate does not, and treating one as the other is the most expensive confusion in this area.

quizzes.q: What is the difference between price and cost?
options: Price applies to goods and cost to services
Cost is what is asked; price is what is paid
Price is what is asked; cost is what is actually paid
quizzes.a: Price is what is asked; cost is what is actually paid
quizzes.why: A low price can be a high cost, if the item fails and has to be replaced. Value is a third thing — what it is worth to you.

quizzes.q: Your warranty is cancelled because you opened the unit. Which word applies?
quizzes.why: Void means cancelled, usually because a condition was broken. Expired means it simply ran out of time, which is a different situation with different arguments available.

quizzes.q: What are the five parts of an effective complaint?
quizzes.why: They go in that order, and the last two decide the outcome. The remedy is the part almost everybody leaves out.

quizzes.q: Why is please sort this out not a remedy?
options: There is nothing specific for the recipient to agree to
quizzes.a: There is nothing specific for the recipient to agree to
quizzes.why: It expresses dissatisfaction rather than making a request, which is why an apology is a complete answer to it.

quizzes.q: Why does a complaint need a deadline?
options: Because it is a legal requirement
To show you are in a hurry
Because without one it can be left indefinitely and nobody has done anything wrong
quizzes.a: Because without one it can be left indefinitely and nobody has done anything wrong
quizzes.why: A date converts silence into a fact you can point to later, which is what makes escalation possible.

quizzes.q: Why is an angry complaint easier to refuse?
options: Anger gives the recipient something to answer other than the facts
quizzes.a: Anger gives the recipient something to answer other than the facts
quizzes.why: If they can reply to your tone, they never have to reply to your claim. Calm is tactics here rather than politeness.

quizzes.q: The first reply to your complaint is inadequate. What is the correct next step?
options: Send the same complaint more strongly worded
Send the same complaint to a named person one level up, with the correspondence attached
Wait and send it again in a month
quizzes.a: Send the same complaint to a named person one level up, with the correspondence attached
quizzes.why: Repetition is not escalation, and repetition is what most people do. It is the commonest reason a legitimate complaint stops.

quizzes.q: Letter A in Reading 3 describes a real problem and receives only an apology. Why?
options: It was sent to the wrong department
It asks for nothing specific, so an apology answers it completely
quizzes.a: It asks for nothing specific, so an apology answers it completely
quizzes.why: There is no claim to accept or refuse. The reply was not evasive — the request was absent, which is the most uncomfortable finding in the unit.

teacherNotes.note: Three pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key or an explicit no-key note with a what-most-people-find finding. Practice 3 is the diagnostic and it is built as six remedies and six non-remedies, with every non-remedy rewritten in the key so the learner sees what specificity looks like.

teacherNotes.type: Card 3 is worth more than the other two combined
teacherNotes.note: Partitives and contract vocabulary are useful; the five-part complaint changes outcomes. Practice 6 asks learners to audit a complaint they actually sent, and the finding is consistently the same — the reply they received was a complete and reasonable answer to the letter they wrote, because the letter asked for nothing. That is uncomfortable and it is the most useful thing in the unit.

Learners are vague here because they do not know what the available options are. Repair, replacement, refund, partial refund, reimbursement of a named cost, compensation for a named consequence, written commitment. Seven items, and choosing one is the difference between a request and a mood. Practice 3 number 11 also makes the point that an apology is not a remedy, which surprises people.

teacherNotes.type: Calm is presented as tactics, not manners
teacherNotes.note: Reading 2 argues that an angry complaint is easier to refuse because it gives the recipient something to answer other than the facts. That argument persuades learners who would dismiss a politeness rule, and it connects directly to Unit 7's point about tone. Speaking 5 and Writing 1's extension both use adjective-counting as the concrete measure.

teacherNotes.type: Escalation is the commonest real-world error
teacherNotes.note: Almost everybody escalates by rewriting the same complaint more forcefully, which is repetition rather than escalation. Writing 2 requires the remedy to be restated word for word and asks learners to list what they changed — if more than four things differ, they have rewritten rather than escalated. The extension asks them to produce the angry version and identify what a recipient could answer in it.

teacherNotes.type: Quotation versus estimate is the expensive one
teacherNotes.note: It is a vocabulary distinction with a direct financial consequence, and the two words are similar enough that learners lose it. Practice 2 numbers 2 and 3 are adjacent for that reason, and Practice 5 sends learners to real terms where the exclusions and the liability limit are almost always harder to find than the promise.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Practice 5 sends learners to real contracts, warranties or insurance policies, and Practice 6 asks them to work from a complaint they actually sent: order numbers, account references, addresses, amounts and the names of any company or individual must never be collected, shared or entered into the app. Writing 1 says the complaint may be invented, and that option should stay. Practice 6 asks only which of the five parts were present and how many adjectives there were, not the content.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say a large amount of money and a large number of invoices without swapping them.
I can tell a quotation from an estimate and know which one fixes the price.
I can ask for a specific remedy by a specific date instead of asking for it to be sorted out.
I can tell why a complaint failed, and escalate without rewriting it more angrily.

assignment.title: A complaint that asks for something, and its escalation
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record the five parts of a complaint aloud for three different problems, one sentence each, then record the telephone exchange from Speaking 4 stating the remedy before being transferred and asking for a reference and a date. Second, write the full five-part complaint from Writing 1 with at least four checkable facts and no adjectives in the problem statement, write the invented inadequate reply and the escalation from Writing 2 with its three lines of commentary, and add your full-sentence answers to the five questions in Writing 3 including the rewritten Letter A. Keep everything together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written work
